stages.title: See what Whiteout does and how a round plays

screens.title: Look at a round of Whiteout, from the first word to the score

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know how a round of Whiteout plays and how it scores.
Whiteout is a hidden-word game. It is on Slieve Bearnagh, the fifth place on the Summit Ready map.
You choose any 4 of the 8 game chapters to build. You may build more than 4 if you have time.
First you build Whiteout exactly as it is in Summit Ready. Then, in stage 5, you change it into a hidden-word game on your own topic.
A round has 4 words. Each word starts as a row of lines, one line for each letter, with a clue above it.
You guess one letter at a time, by clicking a letter button or typing the letter on the keyboard. A right letter shows in every place it comes in the word.

screenshot.alt: Whiteout part-way through a word. The mountain photo is on the left with some cloud over its top. The clue, the word with some letters found, and the wrong-letter count are on the right. The 26 letter buttons are along the bottom, with the tried letters grey
screenshot.cap: Part-way through a word. Two wrong letters have brought the cloud down over the top of the mountain.

blocks.p: A wrong letter brings the cloud down over the mountain photo, one step at a time. Six wrong letters and the cloud hides the whole mountain. That is a whiteout, and the word shows in red.
A word is worth 25 points, less 4 points for each wrong letter, but never less than 5 points. A whiteout scores 0. So the best score for a round is 100 points.

blocks.p: A letter you have tried turns grey and cannot be clicked again. If you type a letter you have already tried, a message says so, and it costs nothing.

words: bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Clue` on a WordClue. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `WordClue.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<WordClue>` is a list that holds WordClue objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
not equal
`!=` means is not equal to. `parts.Length != 2` is true when a line does not have exactly 2 parts.
char
One letter, digit or other character. A `char` is written in single quotes, such as `'A'`.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `letters[0]` is the A button, and `letters[25]` is the Z button.
cast
A type in brackets in front of a value turns the value into that type. `(char)` turns a number into a letter, and `(Button)` treats `sender` as a button.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
panel
A control that holds other controls, or covers part of the window. `pnlFog` is the cloud that comes down over the mountain.
PictureBox
A control that shows a picture. `picPeak` shows the photo of the mountain.
FlowLayoutPanel
A panel that lines up the controls inside it in rows, one after another. `flpLetters` holds the 26 letter buttons.
SetFlowBreak
Tells a FlowLayoutPanel to start a new row after one control.
Controls.Add
Puts a control made in code onto a form or a panel, so it shows.
connect with +=
`b.Click += Letter_Click;` connects the button's Click event to Letter_Click in code. It does the same job as picking the method in the Properties window.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button, or a key typed on the keyboard.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `Letter_Click` is the handler for a click on any of the 26 letter buttons.
sender
Every handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to, such as the letter button that was clicked.
KeyPreview
A form property. When it is True, the form hears every key typed, even when a button in the form is the one selected.
KeyPress
The event that happens when a key that makes a character is typed. `frmWhiteout_KeyPress` is its handler.
Handled
`e.Handled = true;` tells Windows that the key has been dealt with, so no other control acts on it.
ToUpper
Gives a copy in capital letters. `char.ToUpper('e')` gives `'E'`.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
exception
An error that stops your code on the spot. The code then jumps to the nearest `catch` that handles that kind of error.
throw
`throw` starts an exception, which stops the method at once.
try and catch
Code inside `try` runs as normal. If it throws an exception, the code inside `catch` runs in place of a crash.
IndexOf
Finds a letter in some text, and gives its place, counting from 0. It gives -1 when the letter is not there.
Enabled
When a control's Enabled is false, it cannot be clicked.
Height
How tall a control is, in pixels. Whiteout makes the cloud taller with each wrong letter.
new string
`new string(found)` joins an array of chars into one piece of text.
count up with ++
`++` adds 1 to a whole number. `wrong++` means wrong becomes one more than it was.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
Cursor
The mouse pointer's shape over a control. `Cursors.Hand` is a pointing hand.
Focus
`btnNext.Focus()` makes btnNext the control that the Enter key presses.
AddRange
Adds every item of one list to the end of another list in one go.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.

screens.title: Read words.txt, the list of the 14 words and their clues

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what each line of `words.txt` holds.
Whiteout gets its words from a text file, `words.txt`. The file is already in your bin\Debug\Data folder, because `summit-ready-files.zip` put it there in chapter 2.
The file has 14 words, and each round picks 4 of them in a random order. So rounds are usually different.
You do not type `words.txt`. You read it here, so that the code in stage 4 makes sense.

code.title: words.txt: the 14 words, one on each line
code.text:
CAIRN|A pile of stones that marks a path or a summit.
COMPASS|It points north and helps you follow a bearing.
GAITERS|They cover your lower legs and keep mud and water out of your boots.
BEARING|The direction you walk in, measured in degrees with a compass.
CONTOUR|A line on a map joining places of the same height.
SUMMIT|The highest point of a hill or mountain.
WHISTLE|Blow it six times if you need help.
STILE|Steps that let you climb over a wall or a fence.
TORCH|It lights your way if you are still walking after dark.
RIDGE|A long, narrow strip of high ground.
GULLY|A steep, narrow channel cut into the side of a mountain.
SADDLE|The low dip between two summits.
BOTHY|A small, simple shelter in the hills that anyone can use.

partLines: The first word
Each line is one word and its clue, in 2 parts with a bar `|` between them. Part 1, `CAIRN`, is the word, in capital letters. Part 2 is the clue, which shows above the word.
The other 13 words
The other 13 lines have the same 2 parts, in the same order.

box.title: If a file is missing or broken

blocks.p: Whiteout never crashes because a file is missing. This is what you see instead.
If `words.txt` is missing, or has fewer than 4 good lines, no word appears. The clue says **Whiteout needs 4 words in Data\words.txt, each written as WORD|clue.**
If a line of `words.txt` does not have exactly 2 parts, Whiteout skips that line.
If the mountain photo is missing, the photo box is empty. If the cloud picture is missing, the cloud is plain grey.
If a sound is missing, that moment is silent, and the game carries on.
To put a missing file back, you download the [[zip file|1]] again and paste its folders into bin\Debug. When Windows asks about the files you already have, you click **Skip these files**.
Skipping keeps every file you already have, including any file you changed. Only the missing files are copied in.

code.title: WordClue.cs: the WordClue class
code.why: You type the 2 properties, and the 2 lines that put a value into each one, because they are new. The rest reads a file the same way as `LoadAll` in chapter 3, so it comes in the copy.
partLines: The class and its 2 properties
`class WordClue` starts the class. `Word` holds the word, and `Clue` holds its clue. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read each property and change it.
The constructor

This part is the constructor. It runs when code writes `new WordClue(parts)`. `parts` is one line of `words.txt`, already cut into 2 pieces at the bar. The first piece goes into `Word`, and the second piece goes into `Clue`.
The start of LoadAll

`static` means that you call LoadAll on the class itself, as `WordClue.LoadAll()`. LoadAll starts with an empty list. `Files.Data` from chapter 2 gives the full path of `words.txt` in the Data folder. If `words.txt` is not there, LoadAll hands back the empty list, so the game shows a message and does not crash.
Read every line

The StreamReader, which reads a text file one line at a time, opens `words.txt`. The loop goes round once for each line, until the end of the file. `Split('|')` cuts each line at the bar into `parts`. If a line does not have exactly 2 parts, `continue` skips it. Every good line becomes a new WordClue, and `words.Add` puts it on the end of the list.
Close the file and hand back the list
`reader.Close()` closes `words.txt`, so that other programs can open it again. `return words;` hands the full list back to the code that called LoadAll.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, frmWhiteout has the variables that remember the words, the letters and the score while a round plays.
These variables are called [[fields|12]]. They sit at the top of the class, outside every method, so every method in the form can use them.
Every field below is new in this chapter, so you type every one.

code.title: The Whiteout fields
partLines: The words
`words` holds every word that LoadAll reads from `words.txt`. `order` holds the word numbers in a random order. `number` counts the words in this round, from 0 to 3.
This word

`word` is the word being guessed. `found` is an array of chars, one for each letter of the word. A letter not found yet is an underscore, `_`. `tried` collects every letter tried on this word, such as `"EAS"`.
The state of the word
`wrong` counts the wrong letters on this word. `wordOver` turns true once the word is found or lost. `total` adds up the points from every word.
The letter buttons
`letters` is an array with room for 26 buttons, one for each letter from A to Z. The code fills it in when the window opens.
The feedback
`wellLines` and `wrongLines` collect the lines for What went well and What went wrong, one line for each word.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, frmWhiteout makes its own 26 letter buttons, A to Z, in 2 rows of 13.
Dropping 26 buttons from the Toolbox and setting each one would take a long time. So a loop makes them in code, all the same, in a few lines.

code.title: MakeLetters
partLines: A new button each time round
The loop goes round 26 times, once for each letter. Each time, `new Button()` makes a new button in code.
The button's letter

A `char` is stored as a number, and the letters A to Z are numbered in order. So `'A' + i` is the number of the letter `i` places after A. `(char)` turns that number back into a letter, and `ToString()` turns the letter into text.
The button's look
These lines set the same things you set in the Properties window for a dropped button. `Margin` is the gap round the button, 3 pixels on each side.
Connect the click
`+=` connects the button's Click event to Letter_Click, in code. It does the same job as picking the method in the Properties window.
Put the button on the form
`letters[i] = b;` keeps the button in the array. `flpLetters.Controls.Add(b)` puts it in the letter panel, after the one before. After the 13th button, M, `SetFlowBreak` starts a new row.

TryLetter is the heart of the game, and it is long. So you type it in 2 parts. The first part stops part-way through TryLetter, and the second part carries on from there.

code.title: TryLetter, part 1: find the letter
partLines: Is there a word to guess?
If this word is over, or no word was ever shown, TryLetter does nothing.
Tried already?
`tried.IndexOf(letter)` is 0 or more when the letter is in `tried` already. Then `throw` stops TryLetter with a LetterAlreadyTriedException, so the letter costs nothing.
Grey the button
The letter joins `tried`. `letter - 'A'` is the letter's place in the alphabet, from 0 to 25. So `letters[letter - 'A']` is its button, which is turned off and greyed.
Is it in the word?
The loop looks at every letter of the word. Each place where the letter matches gets the letter in `found`, and `inWord` turns true. So a letter that comes twice shows in both places.

code.title: TryLetter, part 2, then WordPoints
partLines: A right letter
The key sound plays, and ShowFound shows the new letters. `new string(found)` joins the chars in `found` into one word. If it is the whole word, the word is solved.
A wrong letter

Six wrong letters
lblWrong shows the new count. At 6 wrong letters the cloud is 360 pixels tall, which covers the whole photo, and Whiteout runs.
WordPoints
A whiteout scores 0. Otherwise a word scores 25, take away 4 for each wrong letter. If that comes to less than 5, it scores 5.

screens.title: Choose your own words, and 2 more things to change

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you have chosen your own words, and 2 more things to change.
Your own game keeps the Whiteout code, but uses your own topic. Each word is one word with a clue, so any topic with key words works.
Science: the name of a part of a cell or a plant, with what it does as the clue.
Computing: a key word such as ROUTER or BINARY, with its meaning as the clue.
Spanish or French: a word in the language, with its English meaning as the clue.
Each word must be one word, using only the letters A to Z, with no spaces. Keep each word to 9 letters or fewer, so it fits on the screen.
You need at least 4 words, because a round uses 4. More is better, so the rounds differ.
Change at least 2 more things as well, so that your game plays differently from Whiteout. For example, change the number of wrong letters allowed, the points, the number of words or the pictures.
Every picture and sound you use must be free to use. Add a line for each one to `credits.txt`, so its maker gets the credit. Say who made it, its licence (the rules for using it) and a link.

glossary: bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Clue` on a WordClue. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `WordClue.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<WordClue>` is a list that holds WordClue objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
not equal
`!=` means is not equal to. `parts.Length != 2` is true when a line does not have exactly 2 parts.
char
One letter, digit or other character. A `char` is written in single quotes, such as `'A'`.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `letters[0]` is the A button, and `letters[25]` is the Z button.
cast
A type in brackets in front of a value turns the value into that type. `(char)` turns a number into a letter, and `(Button)` treats `sender` as a button.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
panel
A control that holds other controls, or covers part of the window. `pnlFog` is the cloud that comes down over the mountain.
PictureBox
A control that shows a picture. `picPeak` shows the photo of the mountain.
FlowLayoutPanel
A panel that lines up the controls inside it in rows, one after another. `flpLetters` holds the 26 letter buttons.
SetFlowBreak
Tells a FlowLayoutPanel to start a new row after one control.
Controls.Add
Puts a control made in code onto a form or a panel, so it shows.
connect with +=
`b.Click += Letter_Click;` connects the button's Click event to Letter_Click in code. It does the same job as picking the method in the Properties window.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button, or a key typed on the keyboard.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `Letter_Click` is the handler for a click on any of the 26 letter buttons.
sender
Every handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to, such as the letter button that was clicked.
KeyPreview
A form property. When it is True, the form hears every key typed, even when a button in the form is the one selected.
KeyPress
The event that happens when a key that makes a character is typed. `frmWhiteout_KeyPress` is its handler.
Handled
`e.Handled = true;` tells Windows that the key has been dealt with, so no other control acts on it.
ToUpper
Gives a copy in capital letters. `char.ToUpper('e')` gives `'E'`.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
exception
An error that stops your code on the spot. The code then jumps to the nearest `catch` that handles that kind of error.
throw
`throw` starts an exception, which stops the method at once.
try and catch
Code inside `try` runs as normal. If it throws an exception, the code inside `catch` runs in place of a crash.
IndexOf
Finds a letter in some text, and gives its place, counting from 0. It gives -1 when the letter is not there.
Enabled
When a control's Enabled is false, it cannot be clicked.
Height
How tall a control is, in pixels. Whiteout makes the cloud taller with each wrong letter.
new string
`new string(found)` joins an array of chars into one piece of text.
count up with ++
`++` adds 1 to a whole number. `wrong++` means wrong becomes one more than it was.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
Cursor
The mouse pointer's shape over a control. `Cursors.Hand` is a pointing hand.
Focus
`btnNext.Focus()` makes btnNext the control that the Enter key presses.
AddRange
Adds every item of one list to the end of another list in one go.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.
